extracted.intended_audience: authors, journal editors, publishers, and researchers concerned with AI use in peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative criteria for authors and editors who suspect that peer review reports were produced or assisted by large language models (LLMs), including how to detect, document, investigate, escalate, and prevent undisclosed AI use in peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check publication policies and lead the conversation in advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should take the lead in advance by checking journal or conference policies. Authors concerned about LLM use in peer review should address the topic with editors beforehand, when policies are not clearly stated online or in submissions materials. If allowed by editors, consider adding a disclaimer to submitted work indicating that it may not be ingested into LLMs or analyzed by AI during the process, as a way to put reviewers on notice about the author’s position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical step before submission: review journal/conference webpages and submission materials for LLM policies; proactively raise the issue with editors; include an explicit disclaimer about non-ingestion where permitted, to signal the author's expectations and consent boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of any LLM use in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Any AI use in peer review should be declared to all relevant stakeholders (as stated by COPE and EASE). Reviewers and authors alike must declare how any LLM was used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should require explicit disclosure from reviewers (and authors where relevant) describing whether and how LLMs were used (generation, translation, editing, prompts used, portions of text affected). This helps interpret review provenance and maintain legitimacy of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit inputting author work into language models (confidentiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines (e.g., JAMA, The Lancet) indicate that reviewers are prohibited from inputting author work into language models as this would violate confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ingestion of submitted manuscripts into commercial LLM platforms as a confidentiality and intellectual property risk. Editors should explicitly forbid such practices and communicate this to reviewers; reviewers should be informed that uploading author content to LLMs is unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require transparent journal policies on acceptable AI use
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear guidance is needed from journals on what AI use is acceptable in peer review and what is not—multiply beneficial, in that journals state their policies, reviewers know what is expected from them, and authors may choose to submit only to journals whose values align with their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish detailed, accessible LLM-in-peer-review policies that specify permitted/forbidden actions (e.g., whether proofreading is allowed), disclosure formats, investigatory procedures, and consequences for undisclosed use. Policies should be easy to find at submission and commissioning stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never (or strongly discourage) using generative AI to draft review reports
rubrics_metrics.description: STM recommends that reviewers should 'never' use generative AI in drafting review reports, discouraging even its basic proofreading functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may adopt a strict prohibition on generative-AI-authored review text, or at minimum require explicit disclosure and limits on permissible AI assistance. Consider prohibiting AI drafting because minimal AI use can cast doubt over the entire review's legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require specification of prompts and AI workflow where used (example: The Lancet)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of The Lancet, authors themselves must even specify the individual prompts used and for which portions of the manuscript; analogous transparency can apply to reviewers when AI is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If AI is permitted for certain tasks (e.g., translation), require documentation of the exact prompts, model used, and which text segments were affected so the provenance of content is auditable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt open peer review / signed evaluation to increase accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review where author and reviewer identities are declared would ensure transparency and accountability for scholarly assessment in the AI era. Signed, non-anonymous evaluation is the surest and most responsible way to safeguard against AI misconduct in peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider de-anonymizing reviewers or offering open review options to make individuals responsible for their evaluations; weigh this against discipline-specific concerns and power dynamics. Open review reduces anonymity-enabled misuse but does not fully eliminate AI-related risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow flexibility on the language of review reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers could be encouraged to respond in whatever language they feel most comfortable in, so long as translation resources are available as needed to editors and authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can improve sociolinguistic equity and potentially reduce reliance on LLMs for language correction or translation. Journals should provide or arrange translation resources rather than rely on reviewers to use LLM translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put authors and reviewers into contact without delay when disputes arise
rubrics_metrics.description: Where disputes arise, put authors and reviewers into contact without delay. As a matter of fairness, and in acknowledgment that peer review ought to be a dialogue among equals rather than a top-down imposition of power, if an author disputes an anonymous review, they should promptly be put into contact with the reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitate direct, timely communication or mediated exchange so reviewers can clarify points, supply control samples, or respond to questions—this may defuse tensions and provide evidence about provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should amass evidence immediately when suspecting LLM use
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of suspicion of LLM use, do not rely on the journal to take the lead in substantiating the claim. Run simulations in various LLMs, using the peer review prompts with your paper, to see if responses correspond. Compare the language used to published studies describing AI text patterns. If you run the reviews through online AI detectors, proceed with caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect line-by-line annotations and specific questions for reviewers; save all communications and review texts; run controlled ChatGPT (and other LLM) simulations; compare to known LLM patterns and to reviewers' prior writing if available; use multiple tools and document methodology for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clues to identify AI-generated review text
rubrics_metrics.description: Clues to AI review generation may include generic, formulaic, verbose, repetitive text, written omnisciently from the third person and flawlessly in terms of orthographic norms, and focusing on form at the expense of argumentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for vagueness, lack of specific engagement with arguments, repetitive/boilerplate phrasing, improbable fluency from supposed non-native reviewers, and recommendations focused only on formal composition rather than substantive critique. These are indicative, not definitive, and must be contextualized with other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on online AI detectors
rubrics_metrics.description: For online AI detectors to have validity, they must be controlled against known human and LLM output; only detectors capable of consistently predicting the latter two should be retained. Various detectors ought to be used, to compare among them. However, due to their poor reputation, these tools easily become a distraction, enabling parties to deny their relevance based on the claim that they 'don’t work' and foreclosing debate on the real issue of how to substantiate suspected LLM use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use detectors only as part of a controlled, multi-method investigation (multiple detectors, control corpora, documented settings). Treat detector outputs as relative indications rather than irrefutable proof and triangulate with linguistic analysis and simulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand an investigation protocol from the journal
rubrics_metrics.description: After amassing evidence, inform the editors at once. Concretely, request a detailed protocol — including a timeframe — laying out all steps so that the terms of a potential investigation are transparent. Journal responses should be timely and forthright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for a written timeline and methods (e.g., digital forensics, model simulations, comparison to prior reviews), list of questions reviewers will answer, and an escalation path. If no or an insufficient protocol is provided, escalate quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request reviewers’ voluntary responses and control samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Insist on the role of the individual human reviewers, supplying a list of questions for them to reply to; in the best-case scenario, their response might provide a control sample against which to compare the disputed reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask reviewers to supply a short, contemporaneous sample of their unassisted writing or to explain their workflow and whether they used LLMs; compare stylistic features and content specificity to disputed reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalate if the journal response is lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: If, within a span of days, the investigation protocol is not provided or if it is insufficient, escalate the matter to the full scientific board. Where appropriate, depending on the journal or conference, recourse to outside bodies could serve as an independent backup (such as COPE, ICMJE, EASE, STM, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notify editors-in-chief and scientific boards; consider contacting external oversight organizations if the journal is a member; inform other affected participants (e.g., conference contributors) when higher-level coordination may be involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activate institutional resources when available
rubrics_metrics.description: For affiliated researchers, access to university lawyers, a press relations department or even just colleagues willing to take a stand can help balance the power differential between an individual author alleging material harm and a publisher or the unnamed reviewers on the other end of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use institutional channels to obtain legal, procedural, and reputational support; institutions can help press for transparency and appropriate investigative rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request external oversight and specify recourse options
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of an investigative protocol, ask the journal to specify what, if any, associated external oversight bodies the author might have recourse to if needed. The author noted that mediAzioni is not a member of COPE and therefore they could not appeal to its jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the journal lists or is a member of recognized oversight bodies (e.g., COPE) and that appeals pathways are documented; lack of membership or recourse should be a factor in escalation decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run controlled LLM simulations as part of investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Run simulations in various LLMs, using the peer review prompts with your paper, to see if responses correspond. Compare the anonymous reviewers’ reports with sample reviews they had written prior to the public release of LLMs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document prompt templates, model versions, sampling parameters, and outputs. Use these simulated outputs to compare macro- and micro-level phrasing, argument focus, and structural patterns against disputed reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request a prompt-response timeframe (example: within seventy-two hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: In retrospect the author would have requested to receive, within seventy-two hours, a detailed protocol laying out the proposed steps of the investigation; had one not been provided, they would have escalated sooner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set and insist on concrete, short timeframes for initial investigatory steps (e.g., a 72-hour commitment) so parties cannot delay and so the author knows how to proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: If reviews are unusable due to vagueness, withdraw and pursue accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: If review recommendations are so unspecific as to be unusable in the work of revising a paper, and if portions appear obviously AI generated such that one cannot determine which points are human or machine, the entirety of the reviews may be considered tainted and authors may choose to withdraw the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether review comments give actionable, specific guidance. If not, and if provenance is in doubt, consider withdrawal alongside seeking redress and publicity to preserve scholarly integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go public when reasonable to establish accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are in a position to reasonably do so, share your experience. Through firsthand accounts we should be able to move beyond mere evocations of the 'plausibility' or 'likelihood' of AI use in peer review and to assert, as humans, that this is actually happening — and to hold accountable the individuals responsible for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reputational and professional risks; weigh institutional advice. Publicizing cases can raise awareness and pressure journals to adopt clearer policies, but should be done with documentation and ethical consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remember that authors are the primary stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly publishing involves balancing many competing interests, but authors — not reviewers, editors or readers — are always the primary stakeholders where peer review is concerned. Even if some parties are in favor of automation, many authors will not consent to any AI assessment, especially if it occurs under the guise of 'blind' review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should factor authors' consent and preferences into policy-making around LLM use; authors' rights and expectations of confidentiality and fair evaluation should be central to decisions about acceptable AI use.
